title: robots.txt
definition: A simple text file placed in the root directory of a website that tells search engine crawlers which pages or files they can or cannot request from your site.
simpleExplanation: It's the bouncer at the door of your website. When Googlebot arrives, the very first thing it does is ask for `robots.txt`. If the file says 'Do not enter the /admin/ folder', Googlebot respectfully turns around and skips that folder so your private admin pages don't show up on Google.
realWorldExample: Blocking Google from indexing your `cart` or `checkout` pages. There is no reason a user's shopping cart URL should ever appear in a Google search result.
useCases: Preventing sensitive pages from being indexed
Saving crawl budget by blocking low-value pages

basic: Does `robots.txt` physically prevent hackers from accessing a URL?
intermediate: What does the asterisk (`*`) mean in a User-agent line?

answers.question: Does it block hackers?
answers.answer: Absolutely not. It relies entirely on the 'honor system'. Good bots (Google, Bing) obey it. Malicious bots and hackers completely ignore it. Never use `robots.txt` to hide secret passwords!

answers.question: What does the asterisk mean?
answers.answer: It is a wildcard. `User-agent: *` means 'These rules apply to EVERY search engine bot in the world'.

codeExample:
# Example robots.txt file
# Placed at: https://www.yourwebsite.com/robots.txt

# Target ALL search engines
User-agent: *

# Do not crawl the admin dashboard
Disallow: /admin/

# Do not crawl any user's shopping cart
Disallow: /cart/

# Do not crawl private PDF documents
Disallow: /private-docs/*.pdf

# Explicitly ALLOW them to crawl the public blog
Allow: /blog/

# Tell the bots where your sitemap is located
Sitemap: https://www.yourwebsite.com/sitemap.xml
